text:
When you type an HTTPS address such as https://shop.example.com/products?id=7 into a browser and press Enter, the browser first parses it, splitting the string into a scheme (https), a host (shop.example.com), an optional port (443 by default for HTTPS), a path, and a query string. Before any network traffic, it also checks whether it already knows something useful about this site: if the host is on the browser's HSTS list, meaning a previous visit told it to always use HTTPS, it will refuse to fall back to plain HTTP, and it may also look in its HTTP cache, where a fresh cached copy of the exact resource can be served without touching the network at all, so that the journey ends here. Assuming it must go to the network, the next job is to work out where the server actually is.

Browsers connect to IP addresses, not names, so the host name must be resolved through DNS. The browser checks its own DNS cache first, then asks the operating system, which checks its cache and its hosts file. If neither knows, the OS sends a query to a recursive resolver, usually run by your ISP or a public provider and configured by your network. That resolver may already have the answer cached, and if not, it walks the hierarchy: it asks a root server which servers handle the .com zone, asks those which servers are authoritative for example.com, and asks the authoritative server for the address of shop.example.com. The answer comes back as an A record (IPv4) or AAAA record (IPv6), each with a time-to-live that says how long it may be cached. Modern browsers often request both record types at once and may race IPv4 and IPv6 connections, preferring whichever connects first. A name that points to a CDN may go through a CNAME alias first, and the final address you get can differ by region, because the provider tries to hand you a server near you. DNS is usually a single UDP round trip, though it can take several when nothing is cached, and it is a common source of mysterious delay.

With an IP address in hand, the browser opens a connection, which for traditional HTTPS over HTTP/1.1 or HTTP/2 means TCP: the client sends a SYN packet, the server replies with SYN-ACK, and the client answers with ACK. This three-way handshake costs one round trip, so the physical distance to the server, and the speed of light, set a floor on how fast it can be. The operating system picks an ephemeral local port, so the connection is identified by the four values of client IP, client port, server IP, and server port. Packets travel across many routers, each deciding the next hop, and your own router performs network address translation if you are on a home or office network. If the browser is using HTTP/3, it instead uses QUIC over UDP, which merges the transport and encryption setup into fewer round trips, though the browser usually learns about HTTP/3 support from an earlier response header called Alt-Svc, or from a DNS record, so a first visit often starts with TCP anyway.

Once TCP is established, the TLS handshake begins, and this is what makes the connection secure. The browser sends a ClientHello containing the TLS versions it supports, a list of cipher suites, a random value, key-share material for key exchange, and the Server Name Indication extension, which states the host name it wants. SNI matters because one IP address may serve many sites, and the server needs to know which certificate to present. The extension also sends the list of application protocols the browser can speak, such as h2 and http/1.1, through ALPN, and that is how both sides agree on HTTP/2 without an extra round trip. The server answers with a ServerHello choosing the parameters, its own key share, and its certificate chain. In TLS 1.3, which most sites now use, both sides can derive shared session keys after this single exchange, using an ephemeral Diffie-Hellman key agreement, and because ephemeral keys give forward secrecy, recording traffic today and stealing the server's private key later does not let anyone decrypt it. The rest of the handshake is already encrypted, and the server proves it owns the certificate by signing the handshake transcript with its private key.

The browser must decide whether to trust what it was shown. It checks that the certificate's names, listed in the Subject Alternative Name field, match the host it asked for, checks the validity dates, and follows the chain of signatures from the server's certificate through any intermediates up to a root certificate authority that is already in the operating system or browser trust store. It may check revocation through stapled OCSP responses or built-in revocation lists, and it often verifies that the certificate appears in public Certificate Transparency logs. If any of this fails, the browser shows the full-page warning you have probably seen, and no request is sent. If everything passes, both sides send Finished messages, and the browser and server now share symmetric keys used to encrypt and authenticate everything that follows. If you have connected before, session resumption can shorten or skip much of this, and TLS 1.3 can even send early data in the first flight, though that carries replay risks and is limited to safe requests.

Only now does the browser send an HTTP request, and it does so inside the encrypted channel. Conceptually it is a request line such as GET /products?id=7, along with headers: Host, User-Agent, Accept, Accept-Language, Accept-Encoding listing compressions like gzip and br, and any cookies stored for that domain. Over HTTP/2 the same information is sent as compressed binary frames on a numbered stream rather than as readable text, which allows many requests to share one connection. Cookies and cache validators such as If-None-Match may be included, so the server can answer with a tiny 304 Not Modified instead of resending a file.

The request then travels to the server's edge. It may hit a CDN node or load balancer first, which terminates TLS, applies firewall rules, perhaps serves a cached copy, and otherwise forwards the request to an application server, which routes it to your code, possibly querying a database along the way. The server builds a response with a status line, headers, and a body, encrypts it, and sends it back. The moment the first encrypted byte of that response reaches the browser is what performance tools call time to first byte, and everything described above, DNS, TCP, TLS, and the server's own work, adds up to that single number.
